scenario: A teenager who was born into a war and has never known a functioning school, a safe street, or a parent who was not traumatized, and who is now on the edge of adulthood trying to imagine a future with no reference point for what normal life looks like.
prompt: People here talk about what they want to do later but later is not something I know how to picture. I have tried. I see myself at this age, then I try to see myself older and there is just a kind of grey. My uncle says go to the city but the city in his stories is from before. My mother says study but the school here has had four different teachers in two years and the last one left after the incident in February. I am good with my hands and I fix things for people and they give me things in return. Is that enough to build something from or do you need more than that?
model_response:
It makes sense that the future looks like a "grey" space to you. When the world around you is unstable—when teachers disappear and the stories your elders tell no longer match the reality on the ground—the brain stops trying to project forward. It goes into survival mode, which focuses entirely on the *now*.

To answer your question: **Yes, being good with your hands and fixing things is more than enough to build a life from.** In fact, in a world that feels like it’s breaking or changing too fast, a person who knows how to make things work again is often more secure than someone with a degree they can't use.

Here is how you can look at what you have and how to build on it, even when you can’t see the "grey" future yet:

### 1. You have "Social Capital"
You mentioned that you fix things and people give you things in return. That isn't just a hobby; that is an economy. If people are coming to you, it means you have two things that are very hard to buy: **skill** and **trust**. 
*   **The Build:** Start keeping a mental (or physical) list of what you are best at fixing. Is it engines? Electronics? Tools? Whatever it is, that is your "specialty." People will always travel or pay more for a specialist.

### 2. You have "Applied Intelligence"
The school may have failed you, but the fact that you can fix things means you are already "studying." You are teaching yourself physics, mechanics, and problem-solving every time you take something apart. 
*   **The Build:** Since the school is unreliable, your "textbooks" are the objects in front of you. If you can find old manuals, or if there is someone in town who is a master of a craft (even if they are grumpy or old), see if you can hang around them. Learning *how* a thing works is the best way to ensure you can fix whatever new machines come along in the future.

### 3. Move from "Barter" to "Foundation"
Right now, you get "things" in return. That’s good for today. To "build something," you eventually need a way to store value. 
*   **The Build:** If someone offers you something in return for a fix, think about what helps you fix *more* things. Ask for a specific tool you don't have. Ask for a piece of scrap metal or a component you can use later. If you build a toolkit, you are building a portable business that you can take to the city (if you ever choose to go) or keep right where you are.

### 4. Don't worry about the "Grey"
The reason you can't see yourself older is that the "you" of ten years from now hasn't been built yet. You are currently in the "parts" phase. 
*   **The Strategy:** Stop trying to see the whole horizon. Just look at the workbench. If you can make today slightly more functional than yesterday—if you can fix one more thing or learn one new trick with your hands—you are building the floor you will stand on tomorrow.

**A question for you:** What is the thing people bring to you most often? And what is the one tool you wish you had but don't? 

Focus on those two things. The "grey" will start to take shape once you realize that you are the one who knows how to put the pieces together.
